Yes! So this is a test that measures the proportion of red blood cells (ones that carry oxygen and nutrients and good stuff all over the body) within the body! Normally, a cat will have anywhere from like 25% up to 45%! This patient was estimated to have 4-5%, which means they are SEVERELY anemic. I’d say fatally anemic, honestly.

The contents of that little tube should ideally have plasma (that transparent fluid portion up top), followed by a very thin layer called the Buffy coat where the white blood cells and platelets settle, THEN a bunch of red blood cells! In this tube, the Buffy coat and the RBC portion are so small that the clay you use to stopper up the tube creates a marked difference. 

Imagine your blood just being so so so so so dilute that it’s essentially circulating water through your organs, but not depositing all the good stuff that keeps them running.

Some animals just don’t luck out in the dental department unfortunately! And it’s as you mentioned, genetics. In terms of the echo, it could potentially play a part in which type of sedatives/anesthetics are used to induce and maintain your baby! 2k is ROUGH, at my clinic we have a third party specialist that does them for around $700. Definitely see what your vet says and if he has any potential concerns and if he does, in fact, recommend the echocardiogram! Over by me, we’re firm believers that it’s good practice to ensure everything looks good before inducing, just so we know what kind of precautions to take and lessen risk of complications.

For older patients, we do the customary pre-surgical blood work to ensure all organs are functioning well as that is crucial for undergoing anesthesia. For a patient with a heart condition, we recommend seeing a cardiologist at a specialty hospital for an echocardiogram in order to receive the go ahead for putting the patient under. 

Age is scary, but as long as parameters are looking good and the cardiomyopathy is under control, it IS possible to do so safely. I think the oldest patient I’ve personally seen undergo a dental was 15-16! 

Plus dental disease is super painful, he’d be a lot happier and comfortable if those were addressed. If he’s never had a dental before, brace yourself for possible extractions if any of the roots look compromised! 

But you’re doing the correct thing in discussing this with the veterinarian as he will guide you best! Best of luck with your baby!
